sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: Low-intensity eccentric contractions of the knee extensors and flexors protect against muscle damage
sources.authors: Lin MJ, Chen TC, Chen HL, Wu BH, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Young men in 8 experimental and 2 control groups (13 per group); 30 or 60 low-intensity eccentric contractions (10% of maximal isometric strength) of the knee flexors or extensors 2 days, 1, 2 or 3 weeks before maximal eccentric contractions of the same muscles.
sources.findings: The low-intensity bout caused no measurable damage itself and gave 30-66% protection against damage from the maximal bout when it came 2 days or 1 week before; there was no protection at 2 or 3 weeks.
limitations: Abstract only; maximal isokinetic eccentric contractions damage muscle far more than effort-guided training at 3 reps in reserve; young men only.
counterevidence: The protective window of a low-dose bout was about one week, shorter than after a damaging bout (R6-S48).

sources.title: Damage protective effects conferred by low-intensity eccentric contractions on arm, leg and trunk muscles
sources.authors: Huang MJ, Nosaka K, Wang HS, Tseng KW, Chen HL, Chou TY, Chen TC
sources.population_design_dose: 24 untrained young men (12 per group); 50 eccentric contractions at 10% of maximal isometric strength 2 days before 50 at 80%, for nine muscle groups, against a group without the low-intensity bout.
sources.findings: With the low-intensity bout 2 days before, strength recovered faster (6-31% greater at 5 days) and peak soreness was 36-54% lower after the high-intensity bout, in all nine muscle groups.
limitations: Abstract only; the allocation method is not stated in the abstract; eccentric-only protocols in untrained young men.
counterevidence: The size of the protection differed between muscles.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of typical lower body strength training sessions on sub-maximal running performance and hormonal response
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Sinclair WH, Leicht AS, Deakin GB, Hakkinen K
sources.population_design_dose: 14 resistance-untrained men; two lower-body 6RM sessions one week apart; muscle damage markers and submaximal running at 24 and 48 h after each.
sources.findings: The second bout attenuated creatine kinase, soreness and the loss of jump height at 48 h; submaximal running was impaired for about 24 h after both bouts.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions, far harder than 2 sets at RIR 3.
counterevidence: Running was impaired only up to about 24 h.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance exercises on running performance across 3 bouts
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).

sources.title: Knee position sense and knee flexor neuromuscular function are similarly altered after two submaximal eccentric bouts
sources.authors: Da Silva F, Monjo F, Gioda J, Blain GM, Piponnier E, Corcelle B, Colson SS
sources.population_design_dose: 16 participants; two submaximal unilateral knee-flexor eccentric bouts one week apart, each to a 20% loss of maximal isometric force.
sources.findings: No repeated-bout effect on neuromuscular function or position sense; soreness was present at 24 h.
limitations: Abstract only; fatigue-limited isolated eccentric bouts; outcomes are neuromuscular function and proprioception, not training adaptation; small sample.
counterevidence: A submaximal first bout need not protect at all on these outcomes.

claims.statement: Under reading A no exposure after a phase-reduced re-establishment exceeds the dose the approved rule already gives an exercise re-established with no recent bout at all (at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3, effort-guided under the earlier ceiling), and every later count is at most one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment; the athlete has meanwhile had one more recent bout, whose protection persists for weeks (R6-S48) and is at least partial after a low-intensity bout (R6-S50, R6-S51). Reading A is therefore never less conservative than the approved first-bout rule.
claims.applicability: Recreational adults returning to an exercise after more than return.moderateMaxDays without it; low set counts at RIR >= 3.
limitations: Repeated-bout studies use eccentric or maximal protocols, mostly in young men; no study tests re-establishment schedules.
R6-S50 and R6-S51 are abstract-only and context only.
counterevidence: A reduced first bout protects less than a full one (R7A-S01) and a submaximal bout may not protect at all on some outcomes (R7A-S02); the dominance argument holds even with no protection.

claims.statement: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second, larger bout stayed below that after an unprotected first bout (R7A-S01). Two submaximal eccentric bouts a week apart showed no repeated-bout effect on neuromuscular function and position sense (R7A-S02).
claims.applicability: Indirect: eccentric cycling and isolated eccentric bouts, not resistance training sets.
limitations: Abstract only; small samples; different modalities.
counterevidence: R6-S50 and R6-S51 found 30-66% protection after low-intensity eccentric bouts.

claims.statement: In resistance-untrained men two or more bouts were needed before submaximal running was protected (R6-S55), and running was impaired for about 24 h after each early bout (R6-S54); this applies to the early exposures under both readings and does not distinguish them.
claims.applicability: Hybrid athletes whose strength and running days are close.
limitations: Abstract only; 6RM bouts, heavier than an RIR >= 3 re-establishment.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology is little changed after a strength session (R6-S53, recorded in round 12).

claims.statement: Reading B would let a phase reduction meant for one week also lower the counts of the following unreduced weeks, a double reduction that neither the policy text nor strengthReturnSets states; the extra week at the reduced count has no evidence of benefit.
claims.applicability: Set-count trajectories after consolidation, specific, taper, race-window and post-event weeks.
limitations: Structural argument; R6-S52 shows single sets give smaller gains than three, not the cost of one extra week.
counterevidence: Conservatism alone could favour B; SSCTR-04 rules that conservative does not mean automatically reducing training.

claims.statement: No study tests how fast the number of sets should return after weeks without an exercise; the regain rule stays a conservative heuristic, not a physiological threshold.
claims.applicability: All re-establishments.
limitations: Negative searches in rounds 11 and 12.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime composition rule inside the approved LOAD-ESTABLISHMENT, PLANNED-PROGRESSION and ROTATION envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: The Q1 ruling (reading A: the regain starts from the re-establishment count before its phase reduction) and the whole-count rule carry unchanged to R7A-FREEZE-2, and the runtime meets them wherever the time budget does not bind: my instrument and regain grid give the R7A-FREEZE-1 results exactly. The second cycle changed what a whole week is in one case. QE-R7A-14 made the review read a time-fitted row by its count before the fit, as the projection did; that removes two readings of one week, but in the less conservative direction for the cap. My condition 5 already says a week raises the cap only when its executed sets equal the count before the phase reduction, and a fitted row executed fewer. On R7A-FREEZE-2 the cap now ends while the athlete has executed 2 sets, and when time allows the count returns 2 to 4 at once, which strength.setsAfterReestablishment ("never at once"), PLANNED-PROGRESSION condition 14 and ROTATION condition 10 ("never two at once") and my condition 6 exclude. This is D56: new (introduced by cycle 2), narrow and runtime-only; the record carries, but its binding to R7A-FREEZE-2 has D56 open.

After a performed re-establishment by effort (more than return.moderateMaxDays since the last executed exposure), the earlier count, block-boundary set included, comes back at most one set per executed week, never at once, whatever the state mode at the re-establishment (known load, pending establishment log, unlogged or re-established) (D53, resolved).

The regain base is the re-establishment count before its phase reduction: min(goal sets for the role, 2, the count the exercise would otherwise have that day). A re-establishment reduced by its phase is followed by that count itself, as a phase-reduced return step 2 is followed by the step-2 count (Q1, reading A).

The cap rises by one set only after a week whose last executed exposure of the exercise executed its whole count (executed sets equal to its count before the phase reduction, gate ADVANCE or EARNED, a logged set); a week whose executed row was below that count, by its phase or by an in-week fatigue reduction, never raises it. A phase week whose reduction did not bring the row below that count counts as a whole executed week.
Every later count stays at or below the cap, with phase reductions on top, and is never more than one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment.
Load: a logged load at or after the re-establishment becomes the reference only by the existing adoption rules, never above the re-establishment ceiling (D44, D45).
To be declared in the next policy revision: setsAfterReestablishment states the base before the phase reduction and the whole-count rule, in the words of strengthReturnSets.

D56 (required before any freeze is accepted; not met at R7A-FREEZE-2): a time-budget fit is not a phase reduction, but a week executed its whole count only when an executed exposure of the exercise that week executed the count before its phase reduction after its time fit (sets after the fit equal to that count). A week whose executed exposures were all fitted below that count neither raises nor ends the regain cap (after a re-establishment) or the return cap (at and after the end of the return steps), so the next count stays at most one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment or the return. The return ceiling (lastExecutedSets) is already read this way (R20). Regression tests: my D56 timelines (one strength day of 25 minutes, re-establishment in week 7, budget raised to 75 minutes after week 8) and the S6 fitted-regain grid with a raised budget (16 jumps at R7A-FREEZE-2, 0 at R7A-FREEZE-1).

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

confidence.rationale: The runtime behaviour is verified on both runtimes over the round-12 AI grid and a wider phase grid; the ruling rests on a dominance argument plus indirect repeated-bout evidence, with directed counterevidence read at abstract level.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real-athlete outcome.
Repeated-bout evidence is indirect (eccentric protocols, young men).
Literature access: Europe PMC returned HTTP 503; PubMed used; two abstracts read, no new full text.

answers.answer: Yes: the re-establishment envelope is adequate at this runtime for every state mode; the one-set-per-week regain holds and the event doses hold (record R7A-SSCTR-REESTABLISH-PHASE).
The material fact is a performed re-establishment after more than return.moderateMaxDays without the exercise, with its executed count and logged set from the weekly review (completed-work ledger).
KEEP of the runtime is defensible; unknown is how much protection a reduced first bout leaves for this athlete.
Against reading B, reading A changes the count one week sooner after a phase-reduced re-establishment; neither changes the re-establishment dose itself.
The smallest sufficient rule is reading A with the whole-count condition; no runtime change.
Reading B adds a week at one set with no evidence of benefit and double-counts a one-week phase reduction; a fixed hold would ignore executed work.
It protects progression and the stated priority: the count returns at most one set per executed week and never above the approved first-bout dose.

Applicable evidence supports a gradual return after a gap and partial protection from a recent bout (R6-S48, R6-S50, R6-S51); counterevidence (R7A-S01, R7A-S02) does not defeat the dominance argument; no dose number is invented.
Uncertain: individual protection after a 1-set bout; the regain schedule itself is a heuristic (RB-5).
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed for this nonclinical rule; clinical pauses route as before.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: Effects of Short-Term Concurrent Training Cessation on the Energy Cost of Running and Neuromuscular Performances in Middle-Distance Runners
sources.authors: Berryman N, Mujika I, Bosquet L
sources.population_design_dose: 8 middle-distance runners; 8 weeks of plyometric or dynamic weight training added to running, then 4 weeks of running only; no control group.
sources.findings: The improved energy cost of running was kept after 4 weeks without strength training, and the 3000 m time trial improved further (-4.4% from baseline); the authors suggest that stopping explosive strength training could serve as a taper strategy.
sources.locator: Abstract; Discussion (limitations: small sample, no control intervention); Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC7821917.xml).
limitations: Brief report; 8 runners; no control group; explosive strength only.
counterevidence: Strength kept at a low dose through the taper is not tested against stopping it.

sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Directed PubMed search for evidence that a reduced first bout does not protect (two abstracts read, both recorded as counterevidence); round-1 to round-12 sources and searches reused as recorded there. Search snippets were discovery only; findings are taken from full text or, where labelled, abstracts.

claims.statement: A never-performed exercise (a substitute included) first set up after every exercise in use has passed the entry step is established by effort at the low establishment dose (at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3), which the approved envelopes already use for unfamiliar exercises (SUB-6, NR-21); low-volume effort-guided entries are consistent with the position stand (R6-S01).
claims.applicability: Substitutes and new exercises during return step 2.
limitations: Position-stand evidence is mostly from novices; no study of new exercises during a return.
counterevidence: A new main-lift substitute can get 2 sets while the exercises in use are at 1 set in return step 2 (R21).

claims.statement: D55 behaviour required and now met: an exercise first set up in return step 2 earns no block-boundary set from its single establishment exposure and comes back at most one set per executed week; R7A-FREEZE-1 let it rise two sets in the first week after the return steps (2 to 4, 1 to 3). Its repeated-bout protection is least developed exactly then: a novel exercise, two low-volume bouts of the pattern behind it, protection of running needing two or more bouts (R6-S55) and fading over weeks (R6-S48), and a lower-intensity first bout protecting less against soreness after a larger second one (R7A-S01).
claims.applicability: A never-performed exercise, a substitute included, first set up while the exercises in use are in the return steps of a moderate or long return.
limitations: The sporting weight is modest: by the jump week the pattern has had two low-volume bouts; no study tests set progression of a substitute during a return.
R6-S55 and R7A-S01 are abstract-only and support the direction, not a number.
counterevidence: Two bouts of the pattern before the jump week can already give some protection (R6-S54, R6-S55).

claims.statement: A missing repetition count is unknown, not a missed target and not tolerance: the declared rule holds the dose without regression (gates.missingLogs, PP-9, PNL-7); a logged reserve below the prescription minus one is still a missed target.
claims.applicability: All logged strength sets.
limitations: Measurement semantics shared with Product/Data (G03); R6-S32 supports self-reported monitoring, not this rule specifically.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: Holding the set count for one week after an in-week fatigue reduction is conservative and cheap: acute strength-session effects last 24-48 h (R6-S53) and a one-week break in resistance training did not impair adaptations (R6-S45).
claims.applicability: Weeks with a converging- or local-fatigue reduction.
limitations: Trained young adults in R6-S45; no study of holding a set count after a fatigue signal.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: Tapers work by cutting volume while keeping intensity (R6-S14); a missed key session moved into taper or race-window days would add volume there, so moves stay inside one day phase.
claims.applicability: Missed key sessions in the last specific week.
limitations: Trained endurance athletes.
counterevidence: The key stimulus of that session is lost rather than moved.

Item 5: a return-entry week is one in which an exercise in use that week is at the entry step; an exercise not in use (rotated out and still parked at the entry step) has no weight. A never-performed exercise, a substitute included, first prescribed after every exercise in use has passed the entry step is established by effort, at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3, with no load converted, and then progresses as a new exercise (NR-21, SUB-6).

D55 (met at R7A-FREEZE-2): an exercise first set up while the exercises in use are in the return steps of a moderate or long return earns no block-boundary set for the block of the return, as return-entry and return-step exposures do not; after the return steps its count rises at most one set per executed week, up to its normal count (its ceiling under strengthReturnSets), with phase reductions on top. Regression tests: the RS2 scenario (return step 2 in a block-end week, a substitution window) for HYPERTROPHY, STRENGTH and RUNNING_SUPPORT, with EVERY_2_WEEKS (parked exercises) and FIXED rotation.

Item 6: sets logged without repetitions leave the repetition target neither met nor missed; the dose holds without a regression step and repetitions are never adopted from a missing value; a logged reserve below the prescription minus one, or fewer sets than prescribed, remains a missed target.

Item 7: a week whose last executed row of an exercise is below its count before the phase reduction, by its phase or by an in-week fatigue reduction, earns no regain, return-cap or return-ceiling set.
Item 8: a missed session moves only to a later chosen day of the same sport whose day phase, by days to the race, equals its own; no move in taper or race week; race touches and shakeouts never move.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

confidence.rationale: Each item probed on both runtimes, item 5 through the real review path with and without parked exercises; the sporting basis is indirect; D55 rests on the declared return rule and on directional repeated-bout evidence.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only.

answers.answer: Items 6-8 keep the progression, learning and event envelopes adequate. Item 5 keeps the step-2 week adequate but not the week after: the substitute rises two sets at once right after the return steps (D55).

Material facts: which exercises are in use and at which return step; a substitution window; block ends; logged sets with or without repetitions and reserve; in-week fatigue reductions; the day phase by days to the race.
KEEP is defensible for items 6-8 and for the item-5 step-2 dose; it is not defensible for the week after a return-period establishment until D55 is fixed. Unknowns are listed per item (R21).

Against the pre-R7A runtime items 6 and 7 restore or tighten declared rules and item 8 is more conservative; item 5 makes a two-set rise reachable in the common rotation case where the pre-R7A runtime rose one set.
The smallest sufficient change is D55 alone: no block-boundary set from a return-period establishment and at most one set per executed week afterwards; no policy change.

Keeping the entry dose for every new exercise in step 2 would contradict NR-21; capping the substitute at its slot's return-step count is a larger, undeclared change (R21); removing block credit for every first establishment outside returns is the undeclared R17(c) question.
The D55 fix protects the return principle without slowing the exercises in use, and keeps the substitute's progression as a new exercise at one set per week.
Applicable evidence supports low establishment doses, gradual set increases while repeated-bout protection builds, short holds after fatigue and reduced taper volume; no number is invented.
Uncertain: the individual soreness cost of a two-set rise; whether new exercises during return steps should be capped at their slot's return-step count (R21).
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed; clinical pauses route as before.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Pinero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 39 resistance-trained young men and women; 9-week high-volume program; one group abstained from training for 1 week at the midpoint and then resumed the same program, the other trained continuously.
sources.findings: No appreciable between-group differences in lower-body muscle size, local endurance or power; the continuous group improved isometric and dynamic lower-body strength more than the deload group.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (group allocation, deload at the midpoint); Results; Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC10809978.xml).
limitations: The deload was complete cessation, not a set reduction; resistance-trained young adults; upper-body training unsupervised.
counterevidence: Strength gains were smaller after one week without training, so breaks are not neutral for strength.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).

sources.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus
sources.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of short-term detraining (less than 4 weeks of insufficient training stimulus) in athletes and recently trained individuals.
sources.findings: Short-term cardiorespiratory detraining in highly trained athletes brings a rapid decline in VO2max and blood volume and impaired endurance performance; the changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals; strength declines are limited.
limitations: Narrative review, abstract only; highly trained athletes; no dose rule for the first session back.
counterevidence: Declines are described as rapid in highly trained athletes, so a short break is not free of loss.

sources.title: Effect of short-term training cessation on performance measures in distance runners
sources.authors: Houmard JA, Hortobagyi T, Johns RA, Bruno NJ, Nute CC, Shinebarger MH, Welborn JW
sources.population_design_dose: 12 distance runners; 14 days of training cessation; measures before and after, no control group.
sources.findings: VO2max fell about 4% (61.6 to 58.7 ml/kg/min), time to exhaustion about 9% and submaximal heart rate rose about 6%; running economy did not change; the authors call the VO2max reduction relatively small.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; 14 days, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: Time to exhaustion fell more than VO2max, so performance may drop more than VO2max suggests.

sources.title: Two weeks of detraining reduces cardiopulmonary function and muscular fitness in endurance athletes
sources.authors: Chen YT, Hsieh YY, Ho JY, Lin TY, Lin JC
sources.population_design_dose: 15 endurance-trained men aged 19-26; 2 weeks of detraining; measures before and after.
sources.findings: VO2max, time to exhaustion, maximal stroke volume and knee-extensor strength fell significantly after two weeks; muscle endurance was maintained.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample of young men; two weeks, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: A measurable loss within two weeks argues against treating a short break as no break.

sources.title: Cardiac size and VO2max do not decrease after short-term exercise cessation
sources.authors: Cullinane EM, Sady SP, Vadeboncoeur L, Burke M, Thompson PD
sources.population_design_dose: 15 male competitive distance runners (28 years); 10 days of exercise cessation after 2 weeks of 16 km daily; controlled diet.
sources.findings: Estimated plasma volume fell about 5% and peak exercise heart rate rose about 5%; VO2max, resting heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac dimensions did not change.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; men only; 1986.
counterevidence: Plasma volume and peak heart rate changed within 10 days.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Directed PubMed search on short-term training cessation in endurance athletes, with counterevidence of a measurable loss within two weeks (R7A-S05); round-1 to round-12 and R7A-SSCTR-r1 sources reused verbatim. Search snippets were discovery only; findings are taken from full text or, where labelled, abstracts.

claims.statement: Resistance-training prescription is expressed as a repetition range per goal with load adjusted to effort (R6-S01); keeping the planned repetition target on HOLD and lowering the load on REGRESS keeps the prescription inside that range, while letting a short set become the target walks it below the range (3x1 for a 4-6 repetition goal) with no evidence of benefit.
claims.applicability: Weekly gates of known-load strength rows.
limitations: Position-stand ranges are group-level guidance; the gates are declared operational rules.
counterevidence: A load reduction alone may not restore the target for every athlete; repeated misses still regress the load one step at a time.

claims.statement: A return re-plans every session still ahead of the review, the same day included, under the declared return rule; a session still ahead in a week whose re-entry starts the next week has no declared dose, and waiting is the composition that neither keeps the pre-break dose nor starts re-entry against the declared start rule. At most one session waits.
claims.applicability: Returns reviewed on a day with unreported sessions, and returns whose re-entry starts next week.
limitations: Composition of declared rules; no study tests the first-day dose after a break.
counterevidence: For a short break, waiting removes a session the athlete could do at the resumed dose (R26).

claims.statement: After at most 10 days without running, VO2max was unchanged in distance runners (R7A-S06) and fell about 4% after 14 days (R7A-S04), with larger relative changes in time to exhaustion; two weeks of detraining reduced VO2max and strength in endurance-trained men (R7A-S05), and short-term detraining is rapid in highly trained athletes (R7A-S03). A held quality session at the last executed dose as the first run back after a short break is therefore a missed conservative step, not an escalation (R27).
claims.applicability: Short returns (at most return.shortMaxDays days).
limitations: Abstracts only; small uncontrolled samples, mostly trained men; no study of the first session back.
counterevidence: Measurable cardiopulmonary and strength losses within two weeks (R7A-S05).

claims.statement: Tapers that cut volume while keeping intensity improve endurance performance (R6-S14) and a strength session affects runners for 24-48 h (R6-S53); proximitySemantics counts days to the race whatever the calendar week, so when an event change moves remaining days of the current week into the taper, race-window or post-event days they take those doses, and completed sessions stay as executed.
claims.applicability: Event-date changes that reach the current week.
limitations: Trained endurance athletes in R6-S14; male runners in R6-S53.
counterevidence: A race moved closer shortens preparation; the declared taper doses derive from achieved peaks and do not catch it up.

claims.statement: Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48); each session is judged on its own date (LE-15), so a missed session is moved only to a date where its rows keep their kind, and otherwise is skipped without debt; the next exposure re-establishes by effort.
claims.applicability: Missed strength sessions near the re-establishment window.
limitations: The 28-day window is a declared operational value, not a threshold.
counterevidence: The stimulus of the missed session is lost rather than moved with a re-establishment row.

claims.statement: Holding the count after an in-week fatigue reduction is conservative and cheap (R6-S53, R6-S45), and a return ceiling read from the largest whole count executed after the time fit never exceeds a count executed.
claims.applicability: Fatigue-reduced and time-fitted weeks.
limitations: Trained young adults in R6-S45.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: D56: a week whose executed exposures were all fitted to the time budget below their count did not execute the count the regain or return cap is meant to restore; releasing the cap then lets the count return two sets at once when time allows (2 to 4), the jump the declared regain rule excludes. The repeated-bout reasoning of D53 and D55 applies: protection is partial after low-volume bouts (R6-S48, R6-S55, R7A-S01).
claims.applicability: Re-establishments and returns under a binding time budget.
limitations: R6-S55 and R7A-S01 are abstract-only; the rule is a declared heuristic, not a physiological threshold.
counterevidence: With a constant budget the fitted count stays at 2 and no jump occurs; the jump needs more time later.

claims.statement: Every strength exposure of a return-entry week is at the entry dose (strengthEntryWeek), and low-volume effort-guided entries are consistent with the position stand (R6-S01); rebuilding the remaining days of that week (an equipment change) does not change what kind of week it is.
claims.applicability: Rebuilds of a return-entry week.
limitations: Position-stand evidence is mostly from novices.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: No study tests set-count regain under a time budget, the repetition target after a missed set, or the dose of the first session after a short break; these remain declared heuristics.
limitations: Negative directed searches in R7A-SSCTR-r1 and r2 at abstract level.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: S2, S4, S5 and S7 hold as compositions and readings of declared rules (the gates, proximitySemantics, LE-15 with D52, strengthEntryWeek) and each removes a FREEZE-1 defect with a dose effect. S3 holds for moderate and long returns and for the waiting session; for a short return reported on the morning of a quality day the first quality slot is held but not run easy (R27, non-blocking: no escalation above the last executed dose). S6 holds for the return ceiling (my R20) and for the fatigue reduction; its reading that a time fit is not a reduction does not hold for the regain and return caps, because a fitted week did not execute the count the cap restores (D56, blocking). None of S2-S7 is a new rule that needs a policy declaration; the waiting session and the cap reading are compositions recorded here.
preserve: HOLD repeats the dose and REGRESS lowers the load
Every session still ahead of a return is re-planned by it; executed history stays as executed
Event days follow days to the race whatever the calendar week
Each session is judged on its own date
A fatigue reduction is a reduced week; the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed after the fit
A return-entry week stays one through a rebuild
modify: D56 (runtime only, blocking): the regain and return caps rise or end only after a week in which an executed exposure executed its whole count after its time fit.
R27 (runtime only, non-blocking): in a short return the first quality slot still ahead, the same day included, runs easy.
decision.mec_change_level: No policy change; one blocking runtime change (D56) and one non-blocking runtime change (R27).
decision.trade_off: Fewer missed-set walks below the goal range, re-planned same-day sessions and event days, and no moves across the re-establishment window, against one waiting session after a break and one missed key session per crossing case.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.

S2: on HOLD and REGRESS a log that confirms the known load leaves the repetition target as planned (REGRESS lowers the load one smallest increment, or the repetitions by repStep down to the range floor when no load is known); on ADVANCE or EARNED the logged repetitions may replace it; a newly established load (first establishment or re-establishment by effort) is adopted with the repetitions logged for it. A set without repetitions is unknown, never a missed target.

S3: a return re-plans every session still ahead of the review (later dates, or the same day without an execution report); sessions reported before the review keep their prescription; when re-entry starts the next week, a session still ahead this week waits (rest by design) and never keeps its pre-break dose; a race is never turned into rest.

R27 (non-blocking; not met at R7A-FREEZE-2): in a short return (at most return.shortMaxDays days) the first quality slot still ahead of the review, the same day included, runs easy (R6-NONCLINICAL-RETURN condition 7); until fixed, the same-day short-return case is outside this approval.

S4: when an event change moves any remaining day of the current week into the taper, race-window or post-event days, or the race itself is still ahead this week, those days are re-planned under the new phases by days to the race (proximitySemantics), with completed sessions unchanged; a goal change that only renames a training phase applies from the next week.

S5: a missed session is moved only to a later chosen day of the same sport, in the same day phase, where every strength row keeps its kind on the new date (a known or from-log row never becomes a re-establishment by moving, nor the reverse); otherwise it is skipped without debt.

S6: a fatigue reduction lowers the recorded count and makes the week reduced; the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed that week outside a phase reduction, each exposure counted after its time fit (R20).

D56 (required before any freeze is accepted; not met at R7A-FREEZE-2): a time-budget fit is not a phase reduction, but a week executed its whole count only when an executed exposure of the exercise that week executed the count before its phase reduction after its time fit (sets after the fit equal to that count). A week whose executed exposures were all fitted below that count neither raises nor ends the regain cap (after a re-establishment) or the return cap (at and after the end of the return steps), so the next count stays at most one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment or the return. The return ceiling (lastExecutedSets) is already read this way (R20). Regression tests: my D56 timelines (one strength day of 25 minutes, re-establishment in week 7, budget raised to 75 minutes after week 8) and the S6 fitted-regain grid with a raised budget (16 jumps at R7A-FREEZE-2, 0 at R7A-FREEZE-1).
S7: a week planned as a return-entry week stays one when its remaining days are rebuilt; every new exercise in it gets the entry dose in every time budget and follows the return steps.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

confidence.rationale: Each item is probed on R7A-FREEZE-2 and the reconstructed R7A-FREEZE-1 through the real review path, with twins for S4 and controls for S5; the sporting basis is indirect and partly abstract-level; D56 and R27 rest on the declared rules and my earlier conditions.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real-athlete outcome.
Literature for R27 is abstract-only and not eligible as prescriptive support; R27 is non-blocking.
The weekly-review contract (R18) is assumed throughout.

answers.answer: Adequate for S2-S5, S7 and the S6 ceiling and fatigue parts; not for the S6 cap reading (D56) and the short same-day quality slot (R27).

The material facts are the reviewed logs and gates, the return report and its time, the event-date change, the dates of the missed and target sessions, the row counts before and after the time fit and the fatigue review, all from the completed-work ledger.
KEEP of the frozen behaviour is defensible for S2-S5 and S7; unknown is how often a time-fitted regain week meets more available time.

Against R7A-FREEZE-1 each change is necessary: short sets became targets below the range, same-day sessions kept pre-break doses, BUILD doses stayed inside a new taper, a move could cross the re-establishment window, a rebuilt entry week lost its entry dose.
The smallest sufficient changes are the ones frozen, plus D56 (one predicate for the cap rise) and R27 (one predicate for the short first quality slot).

Keeping the pre-break dose for a waiting session contradicts the return; starting re-entry with one session contradicts the declared start rule; re-deriving a moved session would replace the planned session with a re-establishment.
Yes for S2-S5 and S7: progression is preserved and event priority protected; D56 would let the regain outrun executed work.
Applicable evidence supports the direction (R6-S01, R6-S14, R6-S53, R6-S45, R6-S48); the short-break evidence is abstract-level and only weighs R27; no dose number is invented.
Uncertain: individual tolerance of a held quality session after a short break, and of the regain under time budgets; all values are declared heuristics.
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed for these nonclinical compositions; clinical pauses route as before.
